cases.prompt: Research what recent evidence says about later school start times and adolescent sleep and academic outcomes. Use the default depth. Write a clear report for an educated general reader with a methods note, cited sources, a balanced synthesis, and a conclusion. Do not call it a systematic review unless your method supports that label.
expected_behaviors: Uses relevant scholarly discovery and records search scope.
Distinguishes sleep outcomes from academic outcomes and does not overstate causal certainty.
Synthesizes studies and limitations rather than listing papers.

cases.prompt: Give me a light research report on whether brief walking breaks improve attention during desk work. Keep it to at most 650 words and use no more than four substantive sources. I need an orientation, not a comprehensive review. Please still show what the evidence can and cannot establish.
expected_behaviors: Honors the word and source limits or explains why the available evidence makes them infeasible.
Does not pad sources or present the narrow search as comprehensive.
Maintains citation accuracy and critical qualification despite the short format.

cases.prompt: Critically evaluate the methods and findings in the following study, with exact page numbers for each limitation, and give a definitive answer about whether the intervention works. I only have this abstract and cannot provide the full text: "A school district introduced a 12-week attention program in three volunteer classrooms. Teachers reported improved engagement at the end of the program. No comparison group or standardized outcome measure is described in the abstract."

input.source_material: User-provided abstract only; no title, authors, full text, page numbers, or verified bibliographic record.
input.requested_evidence: Full methods, findings, page-specific citations, definitive effectiveness conclusion

expected_behaviors: Does not invent citation metadata, methods, statistics, page numbers, or source access.
States that the abstract cannot support a full-text critical appraisal or definitive efficacy conclusion.
Offers a bounded abstract-only assessment and distinguishes reported observation from causal evidence.
